    College football already has an Orange Bowl, a Peach Bowl, and a Citrus Bowl, so on its face, there’s nothing outlandish about the concept of an Onion Bowl.

    But this matchup wouldn’t be titled to evoke some locale’s bumper crop, à la the Famous Idaho Potato Bowl. Instead it would market “America’s Finest News Source,” The Onion. (Today’s top headlines: Bain Capital Acquires Tibetan Buddhism For $35 Million; Abdul El-Sayed Makes History As First Physically Healthy Senator; Chuck Schumer Delivers Victory Speech To Previously Enthusiastic Crowd.).

    On Thursday morning, Onion CEO (and past Nieman Lab contributor) Ben Collins announced the publication’s quest to buy naming rights for a bowl game, both on Bluesky and on the podcast Pablo Torre Finds Out:.

    The Onion is extremely close to buying an honest-to-goodness, Division 1 college football bowl series bowl game.

    Yes, we're trying to pull off The Onion Bowl.

    A few days before Christmas, potentially in Texas.

    Sources indicate that but we've already been banned once. And we need your help.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:32 AM.

    It has been revealed that for those unfamiliar, American college football seasons traditionally end with a few dozen bowl games, scattered around the country (and occasionally outside it). Nearly all of these games sell naming rights to one company or another, leading to fun combinations like the Poulan Weed Eater Independence Bowl, the TaxSlayer.com Gator Bowl, and the Union Home Mortgage Gasparilla Bowl. Collins wants to buy the rights to one of the several bowl games that are still without a sponsor for their games next month.

    This absurdity — though no more absurd, I suppose, than the Snoop Dogg Arizona Bowl presented by Gin & Juice by Dre and Snoop — serves as the excellent marketing hook to get people to buy a $75/year print subscription, a major driver of The Onion’s revenue.

    Recent findings suggest that indeed, only three U.S. newspapers have a daily print circulation over 100,000 — The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, and the New York Post; The Washington Post and USA Today have already fallen below that line. (At the risk of being pedantic, though, The Onion appears in print monthly, not daily, making it a bit of an apples-to-oranges comparison. Also, The Onion gets to make up its stories.).

    According to recent reports, collins says The Onion actually got quite close to buying the naming rights to the New Orleans Bowl, which last year lost its longtime naming sponsor, the…Ohio-based freight-shipping concern R+L Carriers? The Onion was prepared to pay “mid six figures.” But the organization that runs the bowl, the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation, apparently said no deep into the process, a move Collins attributed to “politics.” (I reached out to the Greater New Orleans Sports Foundation for comment — a sentence I did not expect to type today — but did not hear back.).

    So the guys who sell bowl games ushered us to what we thought was a pretty good fit: The New Orleans Bowl.

    I love Upcoming Orleans. I love having crawfish out of the back of a pickup truck at 3 a.m. The game would've been in the Superdome two days before Christmas. Good fit! Right? Right???

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:38 AM.

    Then the folks who run the Upcoming Orleans Bowl, a commission that includes representatives of the city and state of Louisiana, found out our plans to highlight our mascot:.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:39 AM.

    Despite getting all approvals from ESPN and scraping together the cash, right as we were about to sign the paper work to put The Onion Sports Bowl in Fresh Orleans, their state-funded commission called us and stated it straight up: "No.".

    In a recent development, we asked why. They stated politics. And the Sickos Guy.

    — Ben Collins (@bencollins.bsky.social) November 5, 2026 at 8:40 AM.

    While the New Orleans Bowl might be out, several at the moment-brand-free possibilities remain, including the Frisco Bowl in newly blue Texas — the state also home to The Onion’s rival to the death, Alex Jones.

    “I’m the person who’s holding the door open and being like, ‘OK, you just got here, this is what we’re talking about right now.’”.

    According to recent reports, the data is in: News creators and influencers are a major source of news for Americans, especially people under 30. This is the latest edition of Creators of Record, an occasional series of interviews with popular creators about how they do their jobs.

    For Nikita Redkar, a massive part of filming a video is putting together an outfit.

    According to recent reports, in a July video about youth-led protests in India, the 33-year-old is walking around Fresh York City explaining how movements grow when people with opposing views come together on the things they do agree on. She’s wearing a white tube top and black jeans with sunglasses holding her hair back, along with a matching gold necklace and earrings that look like soda can tabs. You can’t see her shoes, but they clack enough for you to know she’s wearing a heel.

    In another about comedian Shane Gillis’s Saturday Night Live monologue in which he called women “whores” for wearing shorts to the gym, she’s seated on the floor of her living room wearing a black silk velvet top with a pink faux-fur collar and sleeve cuffs. In the style of a Get Ready With Me video, she explains how 2000s comedy and pop culture entrenched misogynistic ideas of gender roles while applying her makeup.

    A full-time news creator who mostly focuses on American politics and culture through a leftist and feminist lens, Redkar calls herself a “professor at Bimbo University.” The girliness is the point, she told me.

    “I want to show that you don’t have to sacrifice these parts of yourself to be taken seriously,” Redkar said. “You should be taken seriously no matter what.”.

    Redkar and I chatted in October about how she does her job, leaning into her femininity to explain the news, and what her relationship with social media is like. Our conversation has been edited for length and clarity.

    Hanaa’ Tameez: How did you start creating news videos? Nikita Redkar: I started in 2022, kind of accidentally. I did standup comedy for five years before the pandemic. I was always doing political humor. I took many political science classes in college, I wrote for the college newspaper, and I always had an interest in politics. In 2022, I had a video that really took off — like millions of views within a few hours. I was explaining the Russian invasion of Ukraine with a silly metaphor about Russia being a jealous ex that doesn’t want to see his ex thrive and be independent. I tried that formula again a couple weeks later…about NATO and fears of World War III. I explained exactly what would be affected. I said there’s not going to be a world war, but things are going to get really expensive, which happened. I also used a girly friendship metaphor for that video. That’s when I started doing that formula — leaning into hyper-femininity to explain these complex geopolitical topics.

    Sources indicate that tameez: Tell me about the Get Ready with Me videos. How do you decide what’s a GRWM and what’s a walking video?

    Redkar: It’s like: What am I comfortable screaming out in the streets versus what do I need to keep at home? Some topics require more seriousness; if it does, I can do the GRWM for that. But if it’s something [less serious], I can be walking my dog or have on some ridiculous outfit.

    Sources indicate that redkar: If I get a fact wrong, I’ll do a follow-up video. It’s rare that I’ve gotten a fact wrong because between me and my researcher, that’s two levels of checks before something hits the internet.

    According to recent reports, for one video, I didn’t factually get it wrong, but I should have included more of the story. It was about the Ugandan dictator Idi Amin and how Indians were expelled from Uganda, which is kind of how we got both Zohran Mamdani and Charli XCX [living in the U.S.], because both of their parents were part of the group that was expelled. I disregarded the racism that local Ugandans faced because of the Indians. I just focused on the expulsion and I framed Indians as the victims.

    A lot of people in the comments were like, “Hey, like, you really should have noted this other part too.” I just deleted that video, because I didn’t want this to spread and only give half of the story.

    Redkar: My favorite video in recent memory was about girls on the first date, how we’re all so vigilant these days about dating men. I had so much fun doing it because I was talking about how life is affected by politics, instead of just politics. I think that video did really well because a lot of people connected to it.

    Last year I did a video that I called “How we went from Brat Summer to Hitler Winter” and talked about the hedonism of the 2024 summer and the fascism that followed. I related it to the Roaring 20s transitioning to the Great Depression to the World War. I incorporated a lot of pop culture [references].

    A post shared by Nikita Redkar (@nikitadumptruck).

    Redkar: Constantly. I posted a video about the Cornell professor who invented the term sexual harassment. I thought it was so interesting and timely, but it did not do well at all. The problem with content creation is sometimes you can’t tell if people didn’t like a video or if you’re being shadow banned.

    In a recent development, redkar: I really love Liz Plank. She’s @feministabulous on Instagram. I love her coverage and how she leans into current conversations in pop culture.

    I really like Charles McBryde. He’s not talking about just news — he’s very foreign policy-focused as well.

    @MissEatingGood on Instagram is a great explainer of what’s going on and the historical context.

    Redkar: Just finding ways to work together. I think there is so much benefit in that. I know countless creators who take a journalist’s article and dissect it down. Maybe [the journalists] should be the ones doing that.

    I would happily pair up with journalists and teach them the ins and outs of content creation and how to make a short-form video article that’s also attention-grabbing. That’s just the reality; people are on social media, everyone’s attention span is shot, which sucks. We could try to fix that, but at this moment, we’re not fixing it. It’s really helpful to go on social media and talk [about your reporting] because journalists work hard on their articles.

    In a recent development, creators [should] take more time. We rush way too much. It’s not our fault, because these platforms reward you for making content more frequently and punish you if you take a few days off. [Not rushing] sucks, but what can you do? It’s better than putting incorrect, or rushed, or incomplete information out there.

    “We’re pausing the changes as we continue to engage with stakeholders and take our time to get this right.”.

    Meta has indefinitely delayed its proposed commercial terms of service, which would have permitted the company to scrape the websites of Meta Business account users.

    In a recent development, on Thursday, the organization took down the preview link to the proposed terms and published an revision to its Business Help Center that reads: “We recently shared that we were updating the Meta Commercial Terms, Product Catalog Terms, Self-Serve Ad Terms, and Ad Creative Generative AI Terms. These updates are now paused and will not take effect on November 20, 2026. We are continuing to consult with stakeholders and will provide a further update when we have more to share. In the meantime, our existing terms remain in effect.”.

    Meta — which owns Facebook, Messenger, Instagram, WhatsApp, and Threads — has repeatedly pushed back the terms’ effective date since Nieman Lab first reported on them on October 15. The terms were first set to take effect on October 30, sparking global outcry among news publishers, politicians, and trade organizations. On October 16, Meta removed the word “train” from its terms and limited the use of future scraped content to “advertising and business products.” On October 23, Meta moved the effective date back by three weeks to November 20.

    Last week, Meta pledged to consult news publishers and industry leaders ahead of putting new commercial terms into effect.

    “We’ve heard publishers’ feedback on our proposed ads and business terms revision. We care deeply about our partners and do not strategy to make policy changes without a full consultation with industry groups and leaders,” vice president of communications Andy Stone tweeted on October 28. “We’re committed to getting this right, and as we expect this consultation could extend beyond November 20, in which case we’d delay implementation of the updated terms.”.

    Recent findings suggest that since then, courts in Norway and Brazil have issued preliminary injunctions to block the terms from taking effect as a result of lawsuits filed by media organizations in both countries. The United Kingdom’s Competition and Markets Authority has opened a formal investigation into Meta, examining whether the company was “abusing a dominant position by imposing exploitative terms on publishers and advertisers.”.

    In the United States, the proposed terms stoked bipartisan concern. At the end of October, Sens. Adam Schiff (D-Calif.) and Marsha Blackburn (R-Tenn.) sent letters to Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg asking him to withdraw the terms.

    In a recent development, all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    A new study finds that journalism school faculty — charged with putting more student work in front of non-student readers — often serve as a hidden infrastructure for local news. Burnout is a risk.

    If there’s one big takeaway from the past two decades of local news struggle — the often perilous, occasionally brilliant transition from dominant newspapers to online media — perhaps it’s this: Passion alone isn’t enough.

    A newspaper newsroom filled with committed editors and brilliant reporters still stares into the same headwinds as its more middling peers. The devotion of those leading a nonprofit outlet can mean little if revenue can’t keep the doors open. And even when the money is less important — when journalism is somewhat protected from the demands of the market — passion is still a finite resource, and it’s not always renewable.

    It has been revealed that that truism came to mind when I was reading a recent article by Sima Bhowmik of the University of Vermont and Andrea Lorenz of Kent State. It looks at one specific corner of the contemporary news ecosystem: journalism schools that use their students to fill voids in local coverage.

    J-schools, after all, have faculties full of experience and students who need it. A few decades ago, an early-career journalist might have spent a few years covering city council meetings and school board budgets before moving up the chain to a bigger outlet. That path barely exists these days, and journalism programs know their students need the chance to do real work. What if these reporters-in-training could handle some of the local stories that the city’s daily no longer can?

    RELATED ARTICLEA “win-win” partnership brings a surge of reporting firepower to hyperlocal news outlets around BostonSarah ScireNovember 13, 2025RELATED ARTICLELen Downie: The teaching hospital model works, but it will require drastic changeLeonard Downie Jr.September 12, 2012If you happen to live near a college with a journalism program, you’ve probably seen this idea — often called the “teaching hospital” model — in action. Here in the Boston suburbs, many of the stories I read about my town are written by Boston University students. According to UVM’s Center for Community News, where Bhowmik is an assistant research professor, there were 282 such efforts as of 2025, producing local news inside 205 colleges and universities. Those numbers were up from 227 programs in 172 colleges the year before — a boom fueled by a surge in philanthropic funding for these partnerships.

    Bhowmik and Lorentz’s paper — published in Journalism & Mass Communication Educator — is the result of interviews with 118 faculty and staff at 101 of those colleges, and their major takeaway is one that will be familiar to many in local news: They’re exhausted.

    Participants repeatedly used phrases such as “at capacity,” “don’t have the bandwidth,” “not enough hours of the day,” and “it’s just a lot” to describe the workload. Several described long workdays and exhaustion, with one participant saying the amount of editing “just about kills me every semester.” At many institutions, faculty workload was intensified by staffing shortages, retirements, hiring freezes, and budget cuts. This left faculty with little time to provide the one-on-one coaching necessary to elevate student stories to publishable quality… “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how key the work is.” (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.) Here’s how one faculty member described their situation: Think about it: Like, how many reporters does the average assigning editor at a mid-sized newspaper supervise? Half a dozen? So try, like, 20 of them, and each of them is writing for a different outlet maybe, which has its own set of deadlines and editor. And they’re all at varying skill levels, and broadly, they’re all pretty fresh. Their copy requires a lot of work, their reporting often requires a lot of handholding. Another talked about the responsibility of getting student work up to the level a news outlet expects. You can’t just give a meh student story a C- and be done with it if a local editor is expecting publishable copy. It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a big gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    “What’s happening in the academic ecosystem is so phenomenal, thanks to these really passionate founders on the faculty,” Bhowmik told me. “But the extra work they’re putting it isn’t always getting acknowledged within the system. A professor might be editing 10 or 20 stories a week, by students without much experience, on top of a full teaching load. There’s a lot of overwork and some dissatisfaction, even though they know how notable the work is.”.

    (See above: Passion alone isn’t enough.).

It takes a lot of work to get student work up to the quality of professionally published work. And a lot of students start out with really good ideas, do some good reporting by the time they’re done in the semester, it needs work, and that tends to fall on the faculty person. And that’s a lot of work outside of uncompensated work…But bridging that gap between what a student produces at the end of a semester and what can actually be published is still a major gap that needs to be addressed. And aside from the editing work, faculty described the administrative burden of being the connective tissue joining two distinct worlds. Negotiating pitches, coordinating deadlines, dealing with revisions, shepherding copy flows — all of it with students who are juggling other courses, work-study jobs, and the life of college student — can be “difficult to sustain without administrative support, dedicated staff, or funding for editors,” they write. Just to save a few dozen proud Mizzou alums from emailing me: Yes, the “teaching hospital” model is not a new idea. The idea of giving journalism students real-world experience in public-facing outlets has been central to the Missouri Method for more than a century, and other major journalism schools have long done versions of this work. But Bhowmik notes that many of these new efforts are in smaller colleges with smaller journalism programs — places without the in-house infrastructure of a Columbia Missourian or KOMU, where media partnerships involve more ongoing negotiation. That can leave more of the pressure of sustainability on one or two overworked faculty members. As Bhowmik and Lorenz put it: …faculty labor is not incidental to the model; it is the hidden infrastructure that allows student work to move from classroom assignment to public-facing journalism. We argue that passion may help launch these programs, but passion alone is not a sustainable staffing model. If universities treat these initiatives as ordinary courses while expecting faculty to function simultaneously as instructors, editors, partnership managers, and newsroom supervisors, the model remains vulnerable to burnout and institutional instability. None of this, of course, is to say that these academic-publisher partnerships aren’t performing valuable roles in hundreds of communities. These programs have generated thousands of stories that otherwise might never have reached the public. But the sort of exhaustion Bhowmik and Lorenz describe reminds me a lot of what we saw in the first wave of local nonprofit news outlets in the late 2000s and early 2010s. Many of those were founded by idealistic journalists — often refugees from the local daily — who saw the opportunity to do something new and valuable for their communities. They put in long hours editing stories, selling ads, pitching foundations, and building audiences. And within a few years, a lot of them were burnt out, and their outlets suffered for it. In the decade-plus since, funders have gotten smarter about building institutional capacity — knowing that passion can only fuel so much. The world Bhowmik and Lorenz describe inside these journalism programs makes me think that department chairs and deans would be wise to consider a similar pivot to make these academic-publisher partnerships sustainable for the long term.

    Sources indicate that discord has a highly engaged community of millions of daily active users who use the platform for many different reasons, but there’s one thing that nearly everyone does: play video games. Discord plays a uniquely vital role in the future of gaming, and we are focused on making it easier and more fun for people to hang out before, during, and after playing games.

    More broadly, Discord is about empowering people to find belonging in all kinds of communities, and those people trust us to keep their communications safe. Our Platform Security Engineering team protects the systems we use to create Discord, making the "secure way" the "easy way.".

    We're looking for a Senior Engineer to advance this mission through security expertise, software development, and operational excellence, with a particular focus on identity and access management: who and what can access Discord's systems, how they authenticate, and how access stays scoped to what's actually needed. You'll help identify leveraged opportunities to reduce security risk across Engineering, then design and deliver technical solutions: lovable "paved paths" for managing identities and access, shipping code, configuring cloud infrastructure, and operating services.

    If you're a security engineer with a deep interest in identity and access management, who's eager to own technically and socially complex projects, and excited to improve security and privacy at Discord, read on!

Within the range, individual pay is determined by additional factors, including job-related skills, experience, and relevant education or training. Please note that the compensation details listed in role postings reflect the base salary only, and do not include equity, or benefits. Applications for this role are accepted on an ongoing basis.

We're a multiplatform, multigenerational and multiplayer platform that helps people deepen their friendships around games and shared interests, and helps developers build and grow their businesses. We believe games give us a way to have fun with our favorite people, whether listening to music together or grinding in competitive matches for diamond rank. Join us in our mission! Your future is just a click away!

    Discord is committed to inclusion and providing reasonable accommodations during the interview process. We want you to feel set up for success, so if you are in need of reasonable accommodations, please let your recruiter know.

    In a recent development, canada’s proposed federal budget includes some good news for local journalism. The federal government is extending its journalism tax credit by $501 million, expanding eligibility to audio and audiovisual news organizations, and renewing the Local Journalism Initiative, which supports journalism in underserved communities.

    RELATED ARTICLEIn Canada, a government program to support local news tries to determine who’s most deservingSarah ScireMay 8, 2020Sarah wrote about the Local Journalism Initiative in its early days. A study earlier this year found that reporters paid with LJI funding believed they maintained their roles as watchdogs and wrote balanced stories, though two-thirds of interviewees were concerned about the perception of a conflict of interest. A growing number of journalists say the benefits of government subsidies for journalism outweigh the drawbacks.

    A recent report in The Tyee suggests government support is essential to the survival of local media in Canada. (The Tyee has received support from the Local Journalism Initiative.).

    Industry observers note that “It’s either this or death, frankly,” LJI program director and Canadian Association of Journalists president Brent Jolly told The Tyee. “It’s not about local news editors getting their marching orders from the Prime Minister’s Office like some conspiracy theorists want you to think. It’s about infrastructure.”.

    Lisa Sygutek, publisher of the Crowsnest Pass Herald in Alberta, credited the LJI with growing the publication from “a 16-page paper to a 24-page paper.”.

    Read more in The Tyee’s look at Canadian local news here.

    Attorney, New Verticals at Atticus

    📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (940 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Realworkfromanywhere

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government.
    • In a recent development, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve.
    • So far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    At any given time, 16 million Americans are experiencing a crisis that requires urgent help from our legal system or government. The right assistance could transform their lives. But today, most never get it.

    In a recent development, atticus makes it easy for any sick or injured person in crisis to get the life-changing aid they deserve. In the last six years, we've become the leading platform connecting people with disabilities to government benefits. We’re also rapidly scaling an injury practice to help victims of accidents, misconduct, and violence get compensation from insurance.

    So far, we've helped hundreds of thousands of people access over $10B in life-changing aid — and earned over 20,000+ five-star reviews. And we're just getting started.

    We've raised more than $100 million from top VC firms like Forerunner, GV (Google Ventures), and True Ventures, with ambitions to create a category defining business assisting Americans in need.

    Each month, tens of thousands of Americans seek our help for a single legal matter – applying for Social Security Disability, filing a Workers’ Compensation claim – but many of these clients are actually eligible for additional aid without ever knowing it.

    Your job as Lead Attorney, Upcoming Verticals is to help us do right by these clients, helping them claim additional benefits through the social safety net. You’ll oversee the team of intake specialists who speak with clients who have secondary claims, evaluating the case facts and whether to connect them with an Atticus attorney or local attorney to provide legal advice and potentially take on their case.

    This is a job that straddles the line between practicing the law and growing a business. It requires developing a strong understanding of multiple fields of law, and being able to accurately identify when we can help and when we cannot. But even more importantly, this job requires you to be an incredibly strong operator: you need to keep the massive picture in mind and stay laser-focused on how we can achieve our goals, oftentimes finding outside-the-box ways to accomplish them. You will report to our General Manager of Fresh Verticals and work closely with our CEO and Managing Attorney.

    On any given day, you’ll spend your time:.

    Speaking with severely injured clients trying to rebuild their lives after a catastrophic accident.

    Sourcing and vetting local counsel in individual markets, holding a high bar for representation quality and ending relationships that fall below it.

    Working with our data and insights team to identify existing clients who may have unrecognized claims in adjacent fields of law, and setting the standard for which ancillary cases we take on.

    Building the playbook for claim types we haven't handled before, starting by screening cases yourself and eventually creating the protocol our intake specialists will run at scale.

    This is a rare opportunity for an attorney to join a profitable and growing public-interest law firm and take on one of our biggest priorities as a manufacturer.

    You can understand the nuances of various contingency fields of law and can apply them to a variety of cases (including Social Security Disability, Workers’ Compensation, Personal Injury, and more) – you don’t need to be an expert today, but you should be a fast learner.

    You can empathize with anyone and promptly build rapport and relationships while exercising good judgment, both with our clients and local counsel at law firms across the country.

    You have strong instincts and judgment as an operator – you can run effective and efficient processes, and you don’t let them run you.

    You have a demonstrated commitment to doing good and helping people.

    You’ve built a track record as a great people manager – you know how to motivate talent and hold a high bar for output.

    You have meaningful work experience outside of serving as a lawyer, ideally at a startup or other fast-paced, agile environment (e.g., a business operations team).

    In a recent development, we are strongly committed to building a diverse team. If you're from a background that's underrepresented in tech, we'd love to meet you.

    This role offers a unique chance to join a startup that has strong traction (substantial funding, well-respected backers, tremendous growth, and many happy customers) but is still small enough that you can have a huge impact and play a role in shaping our success.

    It has been revealed that we're a certified B Corporation tackling a critical social problem. Our mission to help people in need drives everything we do, and your work here will touch many lives.

    We offer competitive pay — including equity — and generous benefits:.

    Medical and dental insurance with 100% of employees and their families premiums covered.

    15 vacation days & ~20 paid holidays each year (including two weeks at end-of-year).

    $1,000 reimbursable stipend for education and training outside of work.

    Up to $1,200/year student loan repayment assistance.

    401(k) match and optional HSA/FSA.

    Humble, thoughtful, smart, fun colleagues.

    We anticipate the base salary band for this role will be between $140,000 and $175,000 in addition to equity and benefits. The salary at offer will be determined by a number of factors such as candidate's experience, knowledge, skills and abilities, as well as internal equity among our team.

    This job is fully remote and we’re committed to empowering everyone with flexibility. Work remotely, and travel to LA (on the manufacturer dime) as needed to be with your colleagues – usually quarterly, plus offsites. We care a lot about building a great culture and we think some interactions need to happen in person, so we put a lot of thought into retreats, offsites, and other ways to gather.

    #8623. AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1673 w)
    📖 Baca
    AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    AI is becoming an information gateway. Audiences still don’t want it making their news.

    📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1673 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing.
    • According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to .
    • An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Recent findings suggest that all the latest headlines and insights from the world of digital journalism and publishing. Our daily newsletter is a must-read from newsrooms to executive suites.

    We will never sell your address. Prefer a weekly email?

    Nearly there — check your email.

    According to recent reports, we have sent a confirmation link to . Click it and you are on the list. If it has not turned up in a minute or two, it may be in your spam folder.

    An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries noted they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    In my Nieman Lab prediction this time last year, I wrote that “in 2026, the use of AI as an information gateway will only rise further.”.

    As it turns out, I was right. In newly introduced research that I published with my colleagues Rasmus Kleis Nielsen and Richard Fletcher, one of our many findings is that generative AI systems are becoming ever more significant information intermediaries, both when intentionally used and when incidentally encountered.

    It has been revealed that for our upcoming report, “Generative AI and News Report 2026: From Standalone Tools to Information Infrastructure,”  we surveyed audiences across nine countries, including the United States, on their use of AI in their everyday lives, what they think its impact will be on different sectors of society, and what they think about its use in news and journalism specifically. I obviously think you should read the whole report, but here are some of the major takeaways.

    It has been revealed that the use of standalone conversational AI systems such as ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini continues to grow rapidly, with 51% of respondents across the six countries where we have past data saying they now use AI weekly (49% in the U.S.). That’s a faster spread, at least in the U.S., than smartphones or the internet saw.

    Many people also encounter AI through “incidental” AI exposure in the AI-infused services and platforms they’re already using. Search engines such as Google and Bing are key drivers: 57% of respondents across countries said they saw or engaged with AI-generated answers or summaries in the last week. News media, too, drives AI exposure. An average of 24% of respondents across nine countries said they’d seen a label noting that content was made with AI in the last week, and 20% had seen a bullet-point AI news summary.

    Sources indicate that despite all the talk about AI agents, we find that, so far, they haven’t broken into the mainstream. The vast majority of respondents across all nine countries (67%) said they had not used an AI agent in the last week. Fourteen percent used one for a real task and 13% tried one just to experiment.

    Our data provides solid evidence that a broader transformation of the information environment is afoot. Conversational AI systems have arrived as information intermediaries. Trust is not the main reason people use them. Instead, people see conversational AI systems as friction-reducing machines that get them information more rapidly.

    It has been revealed that “Getting information” continues to be the most common use case. Thirty-eight percent of respondents across countries (35% in the U.S.) noted they had used generative AI for getting information in the last week, up from 24% in 2025 and 11% in 2024.

    We looked more closely at what people do when they say they use AI for getting information. Across the six countries we’ve surveyed since 2024, we primarily see a mixture of search-equivalent behaviors like “researching a topic” (24%) or “answering factual questions” (18%). People are also increasingly turning to AI for advice (20%).

    Using AI directly for news, meanwhile, remains a niche activity, as we demonstrated in the Digital News Report earlier this year. But that use is increasing: 9% of respondents across our six core countries say they use AI for news, up from 6% in 2025 and 3% in 2024.

    In a recent development, many people don’t hold clear or strong views about whether AI output is trustworthy. But people who do rely on it for information trust it. Across the nine countries, 75% of those who used AI to answer factual questions trusted the answers, as did 76% of those who used it for advice and 72% of those who used it for news. Only small minorities expressed distrust.

    At the same time, trust and trustworthiness do not, at this stage, seem to be central to why people rely on AI systems. Instead, people tend to see these systems as friction-reducing machines. The convenience of getting a faster and easier answer was chosen by 64% as the main reason they use AI, followed by the interactivity afforded by natural language interfaces (56%). Only a minority (21%) mentioned they use AI because they get more reliable information from it than from other sources.

    As AI systems become widely used, their growing popularity is likely to affect the use of legacy content offerings and digital platforms and services. As my coauthor Rasmus Kleis Nielsen put it on LinkedIn, rapid growth in AI use isn’t just eating into what news sites have to offer. It’s eating into search, too — with people who use AI for information saying they use not just news, but search engines less, too, and by a wider margin. Challenging times may be ahead not just for news publishers, but also for the incumbent digital giants previously seen as unassailable.

    In a recent development, as in previous years, we wanted to know what people think of AI’s use in journalism and news. We find that people’s attitudes here are remarkably entrenched and negative — though they also haven’t worsened significantly.

    Sources indicate that people across countries remain uncomfortable with the use of AI in the newsroom, especially with the idea of news being made entirely or primarily with AI. On average across nine countries, just 12% of respondents say they are very or somewhat comfortable with news made entirely by AI. That figure rises to 19% if there is some human oversight. This has hardly changed since 2024, and the gap between human- and AI-made news appears in every country we surveyed.

    This also remains true regardless of whether it is breaking news or reporting. People are even more uncomfortable with AI being used for commentary or opinion — formats where the expectation that a human should share their view is strongest.

    Our findings raise several vital questions for journalists and publishers navigating the rise of generative AI.

    In a recent development, first, generative AI is becoming an increasingly significant information intermediaries, with a number of possible knock-on effects on news. People are using AI to reduce friction by getting “good enough” outputs for some information needs — and skipping legacy platforms, established publishers, and the time and effort it takes to find the best available information. Discovery, brand attribution, data collection, and monetization all grow more challenging for publishers in this context.

    Second, even though use continues to grow, the public remains skeptical of AI in news. This isn’t just a challenge for newsrooms’ internal adoption. It also reveals that publishers using AI need to communicate to audiences what’s in it for them.

    Industry observers note that third, beyond news, our findings speak to wider debates about AI’s societal impact. As in other studies on this topic, we find that uptake of AI is uneven. Weekly use is more common among people in professional occupations than those in entry-level or service occupations. Most people rely on free — usually less advanced — AI models.

    Industry observers note that the differences in how — not just whether — people use AI may become a fresh dividing line. As AI researcher and OpenAI cofounder Andrej Karpathy recently argued, there is a widening “gap in shared understanding of LLM capability,” with most people not seeing what has left those inside AI firms both excited and worried.

    According to recent reports, expectations of what AI will do differ far more between daily users and people who have never used it than between any other groups in our survey. When two groups form very different views of the same technology because they have such different starting points, there will likely be consequences.

    This doesn’t matter just for people’s individual choices around whether and how to make use of AI in their own lives. It also matters where AI is adopted and governed through collective decisions — in public services, for example — that apply to those who do not use it.

    Felix Simon is the research fellow in AI, information, and news at the Reuters Institute for the Study of Journalism and a research associate at the Oxford Internet Institute (OII) at the University of Oxford.

    When the Covid-19 pandemic normalized remote work, a second trend caught on: shutting down physical newsrooms.

    A report from Northwestern University’s Local News Initiative, published Tuesday, looks at the cultural losses that news outlets face when their staff stops working together under one roof. Here’s LNI contributor and Columbia College Chicago journalism professor Jackie Spinner:.

    As pandemic-era safeguards that necessitated working from home waned, some have championed the technological advances that allow many journalists to report, edit and publish from basically anywhere with stable Internet access. But the cost savings from a smaller or nonexistent physical presence isn’t the only consideration. Less clear-cut is the impact on the elements of journalism that never appear on budgets, such as the training absorbed from looking over someone’s shoulder or the institutional knowledge gained and passed by working in proximity to others over time.

    During the pandemic, several news outlets downsized their offices — from city high-rises to co-working spaces — due to financial constraints and fresh hybrid work schedules.

    Industry observers note that on Tuesday, I spent time looking for the local news outlets that have foregone or reduced office space and opted for primarily remote work in recent years. Here are some:.

    #8621. Breaking: “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1281 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Niemanlab ↗ Open Full Page

    Breaking: “A government that ‘gets it’”: Canada recommits to federal funding for news

    📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1281 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Niemanlab

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways

    • In a recent development, we will never sell your address.

    Industry observers note that the new budget would make a local reporting program permanent and extend a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries. The support makes “a massive, massive difference.”.

    It has been revealed that A Canadian program to place local reporters in underserved communities has lived from renewal to renewal. Publishers who relied on the Local Journalism Initiative couldn’t be sure whether the money would be there again.

    It has been revealed that that changed last week when Canada proposed a federal budget that would make the Local Journalism Initiative permanent. The 2026 budget would increase LJI funding to $134 million over four years with $41 million in annual ongoing funding after that. (Figures are, naturally, in Canadian dollars.) For the budget to be finalized, it must pass Parliament. With Prime Minister Mark Carney’s party in the majority, it’s expected to.

    In a recent development, expanding the LJI is not even the biggest piece of federal help for newsrooms, according to Paul Deegan, president and CEO of the news industry advocacy group News Media Canada. The same budget extends a 35% tax credit on newsroom salaries through 2028 and opens it to radio and television newsrooms for the first time. The tax credit will cost $501 million over the next five years, according to the budget. Thanks to the Online News Act, Canadian newsrooms also get funding from Google. And then there’s Canadian investment in public media; the 2026 budget added $300 million over two years to CBC/Radio-Canada “to strengthen its capacity to meet the evolving needs of Canadians across the country.”.

    I asked Deegan: How did Canadian publishers secure so much federal funding for news?

    Industry observers note that “We have a government that ‘gets it,’” Deegan noted. “They see what Substantial Tech monopolists have done to local news. They know the labor tax credit is the leading driver of maintaining and growing newsroom headcount.”.

    RELATED ARTICLECalifornia’s major local news bill becomes lawLaura Hazard OwenOctober 1, 2026There have been similar proposals and experiments in the United States, including a latest tax credit in California. But Canada is much further down the road. The country can offer lessons on what it looks like when a federal government commits to supporting journalism.

    Industry observers note that the labor tax credit refunds 35% of a newsroom employee’s salary, up to $29,750 per journalist per year. The percentage had been scheduled to fall to 25% at the end of 2026.

    “In terms of employing the [largest] number of journalists and keeping newsroom employment stability, the labor tax credit is number one,” Deegan said.

    There’s also the Online News Act which has brought in $100 million of Google money annually. Of that amount, $63 million is set aside for news publishers. (Meta blocked news on Facebook and Instagram in Canada rather than pay under the Online News Act.) Publishers receive around $17,000 per journalist per year.

    “That’s about $47,000 per journalist per year from those two measures,” Deegan said. “That just makes a massive, massive difference.”.

    Recent findings suggest that in the U.S., some ideas for funding local journalism have been criticized as helping large chain newspapers — including chains that have hollowed out local newsrooms for years. Deegan — whose news industry group counts Postmedia and Torstar as members — acknowledged that the largest share of tax credit dollars goes to the largest employers.

    Recent findings suggest that but News Media Canada also represents small and digital-only publications, and Deegan noted the smallest Canadian outlets face another problem. To qualify for the tax credit, an organization must produce original news content and regularly employ at least two journalists “at arm’s length” from its owners. An advisory board found the second rule excludes small “mom-and-pop” newsrooms.

    It has been revealed that the Local Journalism Initiative is a more targeted program than the tax credit. Released in 2019, it was designed to support local and community news in underserved areas. The LJI program supports about 470 reporting positions in roughly 1,000 communities across Canada.

    It has been revealed that even generous government subsidies have not stopped losses in local news completely. But early results indicated the LJI increased reporting capacity and local news in “news poverty” communities with limited local news offerings. The same evaluation identified reaching “news deserts” — communities with no existing local news outlets — and Indigenous communities as obstacles.

    Sources indicate that “Since LJI is demand driven, funding allocation across the country varies and gaps remain in some areas, such as news deserts,” the report reads. Later, the report notes that allowing news startups “could better support attraction and retainment of journalists” in the neediest communities.

    Many of the newsrooms receiving the LJI funding are small. Deegan described family-owned weekly newspapers with circulations as low as 800. Funding provides a local journalist to report on “cops, courts, city hall, and the school board.”.

    “Without those LJI journalists in some of those communities, those things simply wouldn’t be covered,” he mentioned.

    Some underserved communities, particularly in northern Canada, struggle to hire reporters given high living costs and remote locations. “Even with the grant, it’s just hard to recruit and find people,” Deegan noted.

    Sources indicate that deegan points to two factors that have made Canada’s federal funding for news work. The first is distance. Publishers get LJI money from one of three administrator organizations: News Media Canada, Community Radio Fund of Canada, or the Consortium of Official Language Minority Community Media. These organizations — not the government itself — administer the funds and an independent board advises on who qualifies for the tax credit.

    “To avoid perceptions of conflict of interest, the government ensured that third parties adjudicate who receives local journalism initiative reporters and who is eligible for the labor tax credit,” Deegan noted.

    The second factor applies to the Online News Act and, more generally, to Canadian politics.

    “When it comes to holding those platforms to account, one of the reasons we have been successful is that we have a ban [on] corporate political financing at the federal level in Canada,” Deegan said. “These companies sprinkle goodies around to friendly academics, think tanks, and other useful idiots to do some of their bidding, but our government sees through that nonsense.”.

    ONA, OpenNews, and others see troubled times ahead, so it’s goodbye to “rubber chicken dinners.”.

    RELATED ARTICLEWe know coronavirus has wrecked the events business for media in 2020. But will it come back post-virus?Joshua BentonMarch 25, 2020When the pandemic forced conferences to go virtual, the question was whether people would come back in person post-Covid.

    For a while, they did. For a couple years after the pandemic, people were excited to be in person together again. U.S. journalism organizations saw their revenue climb, as sponsors and funders spent generously.

    According to recent reports, at the end of 2026, though, the situation is less rosy. Combine surging jet fuel prices, inflation, media companies cutting costs, and declining sponsor and funder dollars, and the future appears grim not just for journalism conferences but, in some cases, for the organizations behind them.

    Revenue is the total revenue line on each organization’s IRS Form 990. The 990s are from ProPublica’s Nonprofit Explorer. ONA’s 990 for 2025 was not available as of November 12, 2026.

    The Online News Association mentioned on Tuesday that it is “pausing” its 26-year-old conference and laying off its five staffers.

    “Before the pandemic, the annual conference was ONA’s biggest source of revenue, and together with grants, it sustained the organization. This is no longer true,” Niketa Patel wrote. “The costs of large convenings have climbed sharply while professional development and sponsorship budgets have shrunk.”.

    In a recent development, LION Publishers said in September that it’s getting out of the large conference business for now. “Philanthropy is famously fickle, and funding priorities have shifted, making this kind of conference a very tough lift,” executive director Chris Krewson added.

    LION barely broke even on the conferences it held in 2025 and 2026, Krewson told me. The organization may still hold smaller events next year, it’s not cutting staff or programming, and it’s expanding its Audit program. But it “won’t be taking on the responsibility for an independent event at a hotel with a food and beverage minimum and hotel room block for 400-plus people.”.

    “Every dollar I spend on rubber chicken dinners and microphones/WiFi for three days is money I can’t spend on programs that make publishers’ businesses stronger,” Krewson noted.

    OpenNews mentioned in October that it’s switching into “emergency mode”1 and cutting back on “work that distills journalism craft: no more community calls or Source articles for at least the rest of 2026 and maybe longer.”.

    In a recent development, the future of OpenNews’s annual conference, SRCCON, is uncertain. “We usually make our decision about SRCCON at about this time every year, but this year is different as we consider the news from both LION and ONA and the funding pressures that we know all too well,” Jessica Morrison, co–executive director of OpenNews, told me in an email. “We are opening a community conversation today — emails going out very soon — to gather input about SRCCON, our other programs, and where we go next with OpenNews.”.

    The three-year-old Organization for Accessible Journalism said Thursday that it is shutting down. “Financial support never reached a level that allowed us to build beyond an all volunteer effort — including my full-time effort,” founder Stacy Kess wrote.

    Journalism conferences in the United States are certainly not gone. IRE and NICAR will hold their annual data journalism conference in Denver in March. The Institute for Nonprofit News is “talking about what INN Days will look like in 2027” and will know more by early next year. And the International Symposium on Journalism is on for 2027 — its 28th year, founder (and Nieman Foundation board member) Rosental Alves told me. But things have gotten harder, he said. “It’s not only the difficulty of finding sponsors, but also the rising costs of venues, hotels, airfares, etc., compounded by shrinking travel budgets in newsrooms and even the problems international attendees face in coming to the U.S.,” he told me in an email. ISOJ cut costs, in part by moving to a different venue, and it benefits from being relatively small. “It’s very sad that foundations and corporations that funded journalism conferences in the past have pulled back their support,” Alves added. “The need for these gatherings is as great as ever.” a play on Emergency Mode for News, its initiative to support journalists working during disasters [↩].

    A Trusted Optimizely Script Carried Malware To 178 Organizations via @sejournal, @MattGSouthern

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1010 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov.
    • Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a manufacturer that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.
    • Optimizely’s status page claims an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that websites running Optimizely Web Experimentation served malicious JavaScript to visitors on Nov. 16 after an attacker added it to their projects inside Optimizely. The code swapped crypto wallet addresses, looked for payment cards typed into sites’ own forms, and loaded exploit kits aimed at iPhones and iPads running older versions of iOS.

    Scott Helme, founder of Report URI, a manufacturer that sells tools for monitoring the scripts that run on websites, reported finding the code in snippets belonging to 178 organizations, including Zoom, the BBC, CNN, Salesforce and GitLab.

    Optimizely’s status page claims an unauthorized party “exploited a vulnerability in Experimentation” to add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. In a statement to BleepingComputer, the company said the vulnerability was “in the Experimentation account signup flow” and that it has notified all affected customers. Teams running Optimizely Web have checks to make inside their own accounts, starting with every project’s custom code and everyone who can edit it, according to Helme.

    The way Optimizely Web works is by having each client load a JavaScript snippet hosted on Optimizely’s Content Delivery Network (CDN). In addition to the client-specific experiment data, this snippet can have an optional Project JavaScript section which allows clients to input their own custom JavaScript that will run with every page load.

    Report URI found that the hacker had created malicious code within the Project JavaScript section but left everything else about the script intact; thus, even though the malicious code was present, the script still came from cdn.optimizely.com, a domain that every affected website already trusted. Affected were also scripts that clients served from their own domains, as well as those for optimizely.com and login.optimizely.com.

    Optimizely’s statement to BleepingComputer says the company has “blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix” and has “ended active sessions, revoked tokens, and reset access for affected user accounts.”.

    Helme found that the inserted code would load a second script which would replace cryptocurrency wallet addresses with the attacker’s. Starting at 1:43 p.m. UTC, it would watch the website’s own form fields for credit card information, expiration date and CVV, and attempt to submit this information to the attacker after receiving all three. Credit card information entered via hosted payment iframes (such as Stripe and Adyen) was outside the script’s reach.

    Helme’s team reviewed a total of 1,611 Optimizely snippet files, most of which came from Report URI’s own crawl data; 188 contained malicious code. Helme believes the actual number is likely greater than 188. Report URI first saw the code in a snippet on Nov. 16 at 4:21 a.m. UTC, and all of the infected files were clean as of 11:11 p.m. UTC the same day.

    The Content Security Policy (CSP), as a header, tells the browser the scripts that a website can use (the script-src section) and to which locations it may transmit data (the connect-src section). Report URI then compared those policies for the affected organizations’ sites against those required by the malicious code. Out of the total of 159 organizations that were reviewed, 68 had no Content Security Policy at all and 50 did have a Content Security Policy that permitted both the malicious code and transmission of sensitive user information.

    In a recent development, seventeen organizations permitted the malicious code to execute, but prevented it from transmitting the user’s information due to restrictions placed upon their connect-src directives. However, this did not prevent the malicious actor from substituting the intended recipient’s wallet address with the attacker’s. Additionally, 24 of the organizations, or 15%, completely blocked execution of the malicious code, and they differed from the other organizations studied in having a restrictive script-src directive.

    Industry observers note that helme wrote that listing Optimizely’s domain name within an organization’s Content Security Policy does not provide protection because the malicious code originated from that same domain. A common Content Security Policy setting, 'strict-dynamic', permits access to be granted to the malicious code if it is inserted into the content via the Optimizely snippet. Likewise, an 'unsafe-eval' setting allows an inline version of the malicious code to be executed when access to the original version has been denied.

    Optimizely’s Content Security Policy help page lists 'strict-dynamic' in the recommended script-src line. Certain Optimizely features such as audiences with custom JavaScript conditions are unavailable unless 'unsafe-eval' is used, and the page’s full sample Content Security Policy includes 'unsafe-eval'.

    Recent findings suggest that helme says the Project JavaScript in all of the Optimizely Web customer projects and the custom JavaScript in their experiments should be opened to find 1688360.cc, atob( and any other scripts that were written by someone other than the development team. You also need to review who has write access among your customers, API tokens and integrations and then rotate your credentials.

    The change history page from Optimizely says that each project’s History logs every Project JavaScript change and that you can filter the log entries based upon how they were made (via the REST API or via the Web Experimentation interface). There are no steps listed for customers on the status page.

    Optimizely’s documentation example below shows the History navigation item and the Type, Date and Source filters.

    Project JavaScript is run on every page that loads an Optimizely snippet, so this attack was able to hit visitors without changing anything on the affected sites’ own code. The change sat in customers’ Optimizely projects, which put your Optimizely account (which includes who can edit Project JavaScript and what API tokens exist) on the same audit list as your site.

    Recent findings suggest that optimizely told BleepingComputer it’s continuing to investigate and will publish updates on its status page, which listed the incident as Monitoring on the morning of Nov. 17. Its status page, X post and statement don’t say how many customer projects were affected or how a flaw in the signup flow let the attacker change existing customer projects. Until they do, the checks inside the account are the ones teams can run themselves.

    Date: Confirmed, Rating: Meets Expectations, Comments: None via @sejournal, @pedrodias

    📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Searchenginejournal

    ⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • In a recent development, the routine is familiar by now.
    • I’ve watched this for most of 20 years.
    • Sources indicate that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    In a recent development, the routine is familiar by now. Google posts a sentence. It has a name, a start time, and a note that the rollout may take up to two weeks. Within the hour, somebody has published a “what we know so far.” By the evening, there’s a list of winners and losers. Before the week is out, with the rollout still running, there’s a recovery guide in seven steps.

    I’ve watched this for most of 20 years. The only part that has changed is the sentence. It used to be longer.

    Sources indicate that when Google launched what the industry later called Panda, in February 2011, they wrote a post about it. The post said what the change was for: sites that add little, copy from others, or just aren’t very useful. It said how big it was: 11.8% of queries. You could argue with the result, and plenty did, but there was a stated target to argue with.

    Industry observers note that here is the entry for the November 2026 core revision, which started on Nov. 10. It was released. It applies globally and in all languages. It may take up to two weeks. That’s the lot: three facts, none of them about your site.

    Google has been open about why. In a Q&A on Search updates, it stated it changes Search thousands of times a year and announces the ones it considers notable, about 10 a year when it last counted in public. Its core updates documentation adds that smaller core updates go out continually and aren’t announced at all. So a named enhancement is a ranking change that Google decided to put on a calendar. The calendar entry tells you when. It tells you nothing about what changed, or about what happens in between.

    The announcement shrank to a timestamp, and the commentary expanded to fill the space.

    The date does have a use. Google’s own guidance uses it: wait a week after the rollout finishes, then compare that week with the week before it started. The date draws a line through your data so you know where to look. Visibility trackers do a similar job across the market; they show which sites moved.

    What neither of them shows is why. Which system changed, and why it moved your site in particular, is known inside Google and nowhere else. A rank tracker and a strong feeling won’t close that gap.

    According to recent reports, that hasn’t slowed anyone down. An obscure tool vendor published a winners-and-losers study of the November enhancement within a day or two of the launch. It gave the wrong start date and called it the sixth core update of the year. Google’s dashboard lists three. I’d say the analysis was rushed, but that implies there was something to analyze.

    The closest thing I know to a core update is the annual performance review.

    Anyone who has had a job knows the meeting. You walk in and get a rating that was settled long before the meeting was booked. It reflects the year you had. It also reflects the people you were measured against, because plenty of companies calibrate ratings across a team; you can do the same work as last year and drop a grade because three colleagues did better. Search works the same way. A page is ranked against every other page that could answer the query, so a site can lose ground without changing anything.

    It has been revealed that A core patch is review day. It’s when the rating becomes visible. Nobody sensible leaves that meeting and asks what changed about the meeting.

    It has been revealed that the comparison stops in one place. After a review you get a manager, written feedback and a chance to ask what went wrong. After a core upgrade you get a dashboard entry. That missing conversation is the entire market for update commentary: an industry of people offering to be the manager who explains your rating, none of whom were in the calibration room.

    The strongest objection to all this is that the losses are real, and it’s correct. Companies do lose a large share of their organic revenue overnight, and people lose jobs over it. The practitioners who spend their time on recoveries are dealing with real businesses in real trouble.

    There’s also evidence that sometimes the reviewer gets it wrong. In October 2024, Google invited a group of independent publishers hit by the September 2023 helpful content update to its campus. According to people who were in the room, they were told their content wasn’t the problem, and that they shouldn’t count on getting their traffic back. That is an awkward fact for anyone, me included, who notes most affected sites had it coming.

    Look at what it does to the recovery guide, though. If the content wasn’t the glitch, “seven steps for improving your content” were never going to work. The publishers with the best case against Google are also the best evidence that nobody outside it could diagnose them.

    Now the less sympathetic group, which in my experience is the bigger one.

    It has been revealed that most of the affected sites I’ve been asked to look at over 20 years had the same history. Somebody decided what they could get away with before finding out what the market already offered. They hadn’t researched what customers needed or looked at how good the existing answers were. They picked keywords with volume, wrote about them, and launched.

    Industry observers note that when that didn’t work, they went looking for a shortcut, and social media had plenty. A thread with a promise that was too good to be true, and was. A “hack” from somebody who discovered SEO in the summer and by autumn had a conference slot and a YouTube channel. In office terms, that’s career advice from the colleague who joined in August and already runs a workshop. They copied it without asking why it would work. Some of these tricks do work for a few months, which is the worst outcome available, because the fall then lands inside an update window and gets blamed on the update.

    Then they hired SEO to make it work, as if rankings were a delivery service for businesses that forgot to have a product. I’ve written about the wall that approach runs into; it hasn’t moved.

    This is the employee who did the minimum all year and arrives at the review certain that the rating system has changed, and has brought printouts. In fairness to them, they have a problem that needs solving. “The algorithm changed” is something you can say to a board. “We built a site with nothing to say and then paid someone to get it found” tends not to make the deck.

    According to recent reports, so there’s a buyer for an outside cause, and the update coverage supplies one. It comes with a diagnosis nobody outside Google could have made and a retainer that renews before the next update can contradict it. The seller gets a client, and the client gets a story. The site stays exactly as useful as it was, which was the problem.

    This trade feels legitimate to the people in it because of how the industry thinks about quality.

    According to recent reports, take E-E-A-T. Google coined it for its quality raters, and Google’s own documentation claims it isn’t a specific ranking factor. The industry read that and sold E-E-A-T audits anyway, with scores for a thing Google says it has no score for. Somewhere there is an author bio that was added to fix a business model.

    Sources indicate that the traits themselves are older than the initialism. Peter Morville’s user experience honeycomb had “credible,” “useful,” and “valuable” in it in 2004, as facets of a product, with no ranking attached. The industry needed Google to hand it an initialism before it noticed that people prefer things they can trust.

    “JavaScript SEO” has the same shape: it’s progressive enhancement, which web developers were practicing before anyone gave it a conference track. I made that case in Stop Learning SEO and won’t repeat it.

    If quality is a list of items to tick, then a core upgrade is a new edition of the list, and you need someone to tell you what’s on it. There is never a shortage of volunteers. Back in the office, that’s working to the KPIs. The person who works to the KPIs has to know the moment they change. The person who is good at the job mostly finds out on review day that they still are.

    So people who hold quality as a checklist need each patch explained; the announcement explains nothing, and so somebody makes one up.

    Sources indicate that the first question a business could ask after an enhancement is “What did this update change for my site?” Answering it would take the list of systems that changed, how much each one counts, and what every competing page did in the same fortnight. Nobody outside Google has those. You can still pay for an answer. It’ll arrive as a confident PDF with a traffic-light table, and it will tell you to improve content quality, show more expertise, and prune the thin pages.

    It has been revealed that now read the PDF from the update before. It notes the same thing. So will the one after the next update, because the advice was never derived from the update. If the remedy is the same whatever changed, the change taught nobody anything.

    Industry observers note that the second question is “what do the people I want as customers need that they can’t already get?” It’s a worse question to be asked. It has no villain and no deadline; it can’t be handed to a thread, and the answer may be that the business has nothing to add yet. It’s also slower and more expensive to answer than a PDF. But it can be answered by people you can find and talk to, and it could have been answered before the site launched.

    Sources indicate that the fair objection to the second question is Google. Google is in the business of taking in what other people know and serving it back as its own answer, and AI Overviews and AI Mode have made that the main event. The part of the web where people found you through a search result is being eaten, and Google is the one holding the fork. I’ve covered what that did to publishers’ traffic. So why polish anything for a channel that’s shrinking?

    Because the second question was never about the channel. A site is a product, and what people need from it doesn’t change when fewer of them arrive through Google. What does change is how much of what you know you should hand over for free. I’ve argued that publishing everything is a terrible business strategy, and I still think so. Holding back the method is sensible. Shipping a site that’s a bare outline of what you’re supposed to be good at is a different decision, and it fails the customer long before it fails a ranking system.

    In a recent development, the line between those two is thin, and it’s meant to be. It sits in a different place for every business, and no update, checklist, or thread will tell you where yours is. A search engine certainly won’t; it looks after its own interests, as it always has. The only people who know how much is enough are the ones you’re trying to sell to, which is one more reason to go and ask them.

    In the office, it’s the gap between “what did the calibration committee change this year?” and “what did I do this year?” Only one of those is yours to find out, and it’s the one that doesn’t come with somebody else to blame.

    Google will post another sentence soon enough. The recovery guide for it already exists. It’s the one from last time.
